The surge of 2015, when about 1.3 million people reached Europe to ask for asylum, the most in one year since the Second World War. Most were Syrians fleeing the Syrian civil war, with many others from Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan, Nigeria and Eritrea.

Most came by boat from Turkey to the Greek islands and then walked north through the Balkans. Others crossed the central Mediterranean from Libya, and thousands drowned on the way.

The European Union tried to share the newcomers among its members, but most governments refused large numbers and several closed their borders. Germany under Angela Merkel took the most after it stopped enforcing the Dublin Regulation, the rule that asylum seekers apply in the first EU country they enter. It received over 440,000 applications in 2015. Sweden took even more for its size, while Hungary built a border fence.

In 2016 the EU paid Turkey to stop the crossings, and numbers fell. The crisis grew out of the Syrian refugee crisis and boosted anti-immigrant parties across Europe for years after.
